sections.h2: Ways to sell a St. Charles home
sections.html:
Sellers in St. Charles usually weigh a broker's listing, a sale they run themselves and a cash purchase from an investor. The deciding factors are how much work the house needs, how soon you must close and how you feel about open houses.

Owners live in 68.0% of homes, and the middle value of an owned home is $298,700, so a conventional listing has plenty of natural buyers. Cash makes more sense when repairs would sink a lender-financed deal, when probate or a relocation has set the clock, or when you simply want no showings.

  • Broker listing: strongest for a house in good shape inside a school zone buyers recognize.
  • Owner-handled sale: no broker commission, though negotiating and paperwork fall to you.
  • Investor purchase: the house sells with its flaws, and you negotiate the closing day.

St. Charles is the seat of St. Charles County, set on the Missouri River about 20 miles northwest of downtown St. Louis. Interstate 70 and Missouri routes 370, 94 and 364 all serve the city. Older blocks around Main Street and the riverfront form the St. Charles Historic District, while most of the housing stock came from subdivisions built since the late 1970s.

Families shop by school district, so learn which one applies to your street. The City of St. Charles School District covers most addresses, including St. Charles High and St. Charles West. Southern edges belong to Francis Howell, and Orchard Farm serves the north. A call to the district office settles the assignment for a given house number.

Every residential real estate transaction inside St. Charles requires a city disclosure completed and signed by the seller. It comes from Ordinance 23-062, passed June 6, 2023 and in force since September 1, 2023. After closing, a notarized copy goes to the city. The disclosure does not need to be recorded.

The form gives incoming owners formal notice of local rules. The city lists these topics:

  • Building and sign permits, inspections and fencing
  • RV and boat parking and storage
  • Property maintenance and solid waste collection
  • Short term rentals
  • Historic preservation districts and floodplain development
  • Site plan review, architectural review and zoning classification

Ask your title company to put the disclosure in the closing packet so it is not forgotten. City staff take questions at 636-949-3222.

Long term rentals need a residential occupancy inspection. An approved inspection must be in place before the first tenant moves in and again between each change of tenant. If the house has been rented out, ask Community Development whether the unit's inspection is current.

For an owner-occupied sale, the city's inspection page ties occupancy inspections to rentals, so confirm with Community Development at 636-949-3222 whether anything applies to your address.

New short term rentals are rarely possible now, and almost never in a residential area. On April 15, 2025 the city amended its ordinance, lifting the moratorium but limiting new residential permits to the Extended Historic Preservation District and cutting the cap to 0.15% of housing units, or up to 48 units in residential zones. The city has reached that maximum and is not accepting new applications for residentially zoned short term rentals.

Existing permits renew every year and include a safety inspection, a noise monitoring device, one off-street parking space per rented bedroom and a 500 foot buffer from other residential short term rentals. Commercially zoned properties inside the historic district overlay are treated differently. If a house has operated as a short term rental, ask Community Development to confirm its permit at 636-949-3222, and ask the county at 636-949-7900 how the use affects the tax bill.

sections.h2: Recording a deed in St. Charles
sections.html:
The county Recorder of Deeds, at 201 N. Second Street in St. Charles, files deeds for city properties. Under the fee schedule that took effect August 28, 2026, a standard 8.5 by 11 inch page costs $23.00 and each further page $3.00. Documents that miss the format rules draw an extra $25.00. The office takes cards for a convenience fee and refuses personal checks.

Closing agents usually file the deed and pay from settlement funds. Phone 636-949-7900 if you plan to record something on your own, such as a release of an old lien.

Spring is the wettest season, and buyers near the river or inside the floodplain will ask about water. Check gutters, the basement and the roof before inspections. Floodplain development is also one of the topics on the city's disclosure form, so find out whether your lot falls in a flood zone and be ready to say so.

A house inside the St. Charles Historic District carries extra rules on exterior changes, and buyers who love old brick and narrow streets will ask about them. If your house is on those blocks, find out what approvals past work received and keep the paperwork. A buyer's lender or title company may want to see it.

Houses in the newer subdivisions face fewer design rules, but permits for decks, fences and finished basements still matter. Gather what you have before you list, because missing permits are an easy way to lose a week at the end of the deal.

The city disclosure and the county recording both sit on the closing timeline, so start the local paperwork early.

  • Download the disclosure form from the city's Residential Real Estate Disclosure page and complete it with your title company.
  • Work out whether the house is in the historic district, a floodplain or a residential zone, since each carries its own rules.
  • If the house has been rented, check the long term rental inspection status.
  • Confirm the school district for the address and note it in your marketing.
  • If the house hosted short term guests, ask the county how that affects the tax bill.

A tidy file helps whichever route you choose. With a cash buyer, the sequence is brief: offer, title search, signing, recording and payment. With a financed buyer, expect an appraisal and loan approval in the middle.

faqs.q: Does the city of St. Charles require a seller disclosure?
faqs.a: Yes. Ordinance 23-062 has applied to all residential transactions inside city limits since September 1, 2023. The seller signs the form, a notarized copy goes to the city after closing, and it is not recorded.

faqs.q: What is the St. Charles County deed recording fee?
faqs.a: Since August 28, 2026 the county charges $23.00 for page one and $3.00 for every page after it, and $25.00 more when a document is non-standard.

faqs.q: Which school district is my St. Charles house in?
faqs.a: Most of the city is in the City of St. Charles School District. Southern edges belong to Francis Howell and northern areas to Orchard Farm, so confirm your address with the district office.

faqs.q: Can I turn my St. Charles house into an Airbnb before selling it?
faqs.a: Probably not in a residential zone. The city is at its cap of 0.15% of housing units and is not taking new applications for residentially zoned short term rentals. Call 636-949-3222 to verify zoning.

faqs.q: Do I need an occupancy inspection to sell my St. Charles home?
faqs.a: The city ties occupancy inspections to long term rentals, which need one before the first tenant and between tenants. For an owner-occupied sale, call Community Development at 636-949-3222 to confirm.
